response.description_long:
For a company selling through more than one payment provider, month-end reconciliation turns into a recurring spreadsheet project: export from each processor, VLOOKUP the charges against invoices, and manually untangle fees, refunds, and chargebacks. Ledgerline's own framing is that the volume is not the hard part — the exceptions are. A payout that nets out three refunds and a currency conversion, a chargeback arriving two months after the sale, a processor fee schedule that changed mid-month: each one is an hour in a spreadsheet, and the same ones resurface at every close. Ledgerline was founded in 2021 in New York by Elena Marsh, a former controller who ran month-end close at a multi-processor e-commerce company, and Daniel Okoye, who built payout systems inside a payment processor. Their stated insight was that both sides of the problem — the spreadsheet and the payout file — are already generated by software, and only the matching in between was still manual.

The product is payment reconciliation software. It connects to payment processors and bank accounts through read-only integrations: Stripe, Adyen, and PayPal, with more in private beta, plus bank feeds from over 10,000 institutions. It then posts journal entries to NetSuite, QuickBooks, or Xero through each system's official API, summarized or at transaction level depending on the account. On the money side everything is read-only — Ledgerline states that it reads statements and reports, never initiates a payment, holds a balance, or touches funds in flight.

Technically, the company's bet is narrow and explicit: match at the payout, not the invoice. For every deposit that hits the bank, the matching engine reconstructs the set of charges, refunds, chargebacks, and fees inside it using processor reports and the customer's invoice data. Multi-currency payouts are decomposed with the processor's own conversion rate so FX differences post to the right account rather than disappearing into a rounding line, and partial payments, over-payments, and invoices settled across two payouts are treated as first-class cases rather than edge cases. Every match carries a confidence score; high-confidence matches post automatically under rules the team has approved, and nothing posts silently — the audit trail records which rule matched, who approved it, and when.

Anything the engine cannot match confidently lands in a review queue, which the company treats as the place where a team's judgment gets captured. Each exception displays the payout line, candidate transactions, and the specific mismatch — amount, date, currency, or a missing counterpart — along with a suggested resolution. Accepting the suggestion prompts Ledgerline to offer turning it into a rule, so the same pattern resolves itself next month; the site says customers typically see the exception queue shrink by more than half within three closes as rules accumulate. A close dashboard tracks each processor's status — transactions ingested, matched percentage, exceptions open, entries posted.

Ledgerline sells to e-commerce and subscription companies selling through two or more processors, a group where the company argues pain scales with processor count rather than revenue. It also names marketplaces reconciling per subsidiary via multi-entity support, and accounting firms running it across client books with each client as a separate workspace. The common thread the site describes is a finance team of two to twenty that would rather review exceptions than build VLOOKUPs.

Pricing is usage-based: a flat platform fee plus a per-transaction rate that declines with volume. The platform fee covers unlimited users, all ledger integrations, and support. Crucially, the per-transaction rate is metered on transactions reconciled rather than transactions ingested, and reprocessing after a configuration change is free. Standard integrations carry no implementation fee; there is no annual lock-in, though annual billing earns a discount. The company positions itself against spreadsheets (which "scale until the second processor"), generic RPA (which breaks when report formats change), and ERP reconciliation modules (which match at invoice level and, in its characterization, shrug at payouts).

On traction, the site states that finance teams at over 400 companies use Ledgerline, that customers report closing the books in hours instead of days and month-end close times cut by 70 percent, and that Ledgerline is SOC 2 Type II certified with the report available under NDA. It backfills up to 24 months of processor history, hosts in US data centers, and offers SSO and role-based access on every plan. The company describes itself as 32 people across New York and Toronto, and says it is hiring accounting-minded engineers in both cities. All figures here are the company's own; the site does not name individual customers.
